new_statements.rule_in_words: Shan-Ni/Tai Laing is a tone language (5 tones at Indawgyi, 6 at Myitkyina) and the thesis has no stress section. The only stress statement concerns polysyllabic words: in disyllabic and sesquisyllabic words (and in the grammatical prefixes ma¹ NEG, te¹ FUT, kha¹ DES) the initial minor syllable is unstressed — reduced to C+/ə/ with the mid-level tone 1 — and the final full syllable carries the stress: 'prosodic prominence is word-final'. No statement about stress in monosyllables (the bulk of the lexicon) or in longer compounds.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions. p. 40 hedges the mechanism: the <Cə¹> shape of prefixes and initial syllables 'is probably the result of these syllables being unstressed'. Words in transition have two acceptable shapes (full disyllabic compound vs reduced sesquisyllable, Table 21 p. 47); full compounds show no phonological difference between a word in isolation and as part of a compound (p. 39-40). Tonal system otherwise described in sect. 2.3.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (disyllabic and sesquisyllabic lexical words, plus proclitic-like TAM/negation prefixes with a following word). Indawgyi-lake variety, Kachin State; Owen 2013 (Myitkyina variety) is silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Marseille 2019 calls the language Shan-Ni (Burmese 'red Shan') and states the speakers call themselves Tai Naing or Tai Leng (p. 13); Glottolog cites this thesis under tail1248 and Wikipedia lists Shan-Ni/Tai Leng/Tai Nine as names of Tai Laing (ISO tjl), so identity = tail1248. Marseille's data are the Indawgyi-lake variety (Mohnyin Township, Kachin State), which has 5 tones; Owen 2013 describes the Myitkyina variety (6 tones). No separate glottocode for these varieties.

sources.note: Ch. 2 Phonology (consonants, vowels, 5 tones Indawgyi / 6 Myitkyina, syllables) has no stress section; stress is discussed only for disyllabic/sesquisyllabic words and prefixes: the initial minor syllable (Ca-, level tone 1, vowel reduced to /ə/) is unstressed and 'followed by a full, stressed syllable'; 'The prosodic prominence is word-final' (p. 47, sect. 3.1.2; also p. 40 sect. 2.4, p. 41 Table 18, p. 118 sect. 7.2.1). Nothing on stress in monosyllables or on phrase-level prominence.

sources.note: Silent. Covers 19 initial consonants, allophones, clusters, 10 vowels + 1 diphthong, rimes, script graphs, Gedney tone box with 6 tones in live syllables (Myitkyina data, 2 speakers), comparison with Edmondson's 'Northern Shan'. The words stress/accent/prominence do not occur; the 'Syllable structure' slide is a heading followed by the consonant table.
No phonology; gives alternate names (Tai Leng, Tai Nine, Shan-Ni) and the Leiden handle hdl:1887/74583 for Marseille 2019.
